title_en: OIR/DEF CONTRIBUTION TO NIE-32: EFFECTS OF OPERATIONS IN KOREA ON THE CHINESE COMMUNIST REGIME
title_ko: 국가정보판단서 32호(NIE-32)에 대한 정보조사국(OIR/DEF) 기고문: 조선 작전이 중국공산정권에 미치는 영향
subject_ko: 국무부 정보조사국이 국가정보판단서 32호에 낸 기고문으로, 조선전쟁이 중국공산당 지도부의 결속, 대중의 지지, 내부 반대세력 진압, 중소관계에 미친 영향을 「I. 정치적 영향」이라는 표제 아래 가(A)~라(D) 네 절로 나누어 판단한 문서다. 12장 지면을 모두 다시 읽어, 기존에 「이 문서는 앞선 절 도중에서 시작한다」고 보았던 첫머리가 실제로는 표제(「I. 정치적 영향」·「가. 당 지도부 안의 이견」)부터 온전히 시작한다는 것과, 본문 다수 대목이 실제로는 지면에서 뚜렷이 읽힌다는 것을 확인했다.
key_points_ko: 당 지도부 상층의 「민족주의」·「국제주의」 분파 존재 여부는 확증할 수 없는 문제이지만, 조선전쟁의 경과에 대한 불만이 당 중앙위원회 안의 재정·경제 정책과 마오쩌둥의 「일변도」 정책을 둘러싼 이견을 더 두드러지게 했다고 보았다. 장궈타오(張國燾)는 1938년 중국공산당에서 제명된 인물로 지면에 또렷이 적혀 있다(기존에 「1958년」으로 보았던 것은 OCR 오독이었다).

당·군 지도자들의 공동 이익, 당 조직의 힘, 경제·군사 자원에 대한 중앙집권적 통제, 소련과의 동맹 외에 다른 선택지가 좁아진 사정이 겹쳐 현재의 대외정책에 대한 지지를 오히려 강화하고 있다고 보았고, 소련이 만주 등 더 긴요한 지역이 공격당할 경우를 대비해 군사자원을 계속 대줄 것이라는 확신이 있는 한 당 지도부의 심각한 균열 가능성은 낮다고 판단했다.
농촌 주민 다수는 조선전쟁을 자신들의 당면 문제와 의식적으로 연결짓지 못하는 반면, 도시의 정치적으로 깨어 있는 집단에서는 중국의 참전과 초기 승리가 국가적 자부심을 불러일으켰으나, 이후 군사적 정체는 국내 재건이 위태로워졌다는 우려와 소련에 대한 불신을 함께 낳았다고 보았다.

정권은 조선 개입으로 계획된 정치 강령의 중요한 부분을 수정해야 했지만 통제를 다지는 인력과 행정 기구는 오히려 갖추고 있으며, 간첩·태업·모반·「제국주의자」와의 결탁 등을 처벌하는 억압 조치를 강화하고 인민단체 가입을 늘려 반대세력의 잠재적 거점을 무너뜨리고 있다고 적었다. 다절 말미는 「이런 조치들의 결과로 정권은 활동적인 반대세력을 줄였을 뿐 아니라 잠재적 적대세력에 대응하는 능력도 늘렸다」로 온전히 끝난다(기존에 문장이 중간에서 끊긴 것으로 보았던 자리다).
조선전쟁이 중국공산정권을 서방에서 더 멀어지게 하고 소련에 대한 의존을 키웠으며, 외교·문화·군사·경제 여러 방면에서 중소 관계가 오히려 더 긴밀해지는 조짐이 뚜렷하다고 보았다. 1950년 12월 중소 계획위원회 설치, 1951년 3월 중소 철도협정 체결(기존에 「1952년 3월」로 보았던 것은 오독이었다)을 근거로 들었다.

그럼에도 마오쩌둥이 병력 투입을 매우 꺼렸다는 정보, 중국공산 지도부가 개입 문제를 둘러싸고 갈렸다는 정보, 중국공산 외교관이 「소련의 무기와 자금은 받았지만 소련의 지시는 받아들이지 않았다」는 정보, 베이핑과 모스크바가 지구전과 총공세 사이에서 작전 수행 방식에 이견을 보였다는 정보 등 (1)~(6) 여섯 항목의 정황이 중소 관계에 일정한 긴장을 낳았을 가능성을 보여 준다고 적었다. 다만 이 항목들 다수가 25X1로 삭제되어 세부는 확인되지 않는다.

이런 긴장이 아직 중소동맹의 결속이나 중국공산군의 조선 내 노력을 위협할 만큼 심각해졌다는 확증은 없다고 보았다. 4월 27일 코민포름 기관지에 실리고 5월 3일 중국공산군 방송으로 재방송된 펑전(彭眞, 지면 원문 `P'eng Chen`)의 글을 근거로, 중국공산당이 조선전쟁을 세계 공산주의와 「최대의 적」인 미국이 이끄는 제국주의 사이의 전 지구적 투쟁의 일부로 여기고 있다고 결론지었다(기존에 「worst enemy」로 옮겼던 자리는 지면에 `chief enemy`로, 「expansive view」로 옮겼던 자리는 `subjective view`로 또렷이 찍혀 있다).

I. POLITICAL EFFECTS

A. Disagreement Among Party Leaders

The Korean conflict, by isolating Communist China from the West and driving it to closer dependence on the USSR, has reduced to an academic question speculations regarding the existence of a "Nationalist" and an "Internationalist" clique (for which there is no firm evidence one way or the other) within the Chinese Communist Party. On the other hand, it is probable that dissatisfaction with the course of events in Korea has accentuated certain points of disagreement within the Central Committee arising from disputes over the party's fiscal and economic policies, the postponement of reconstruction efforts, and the intensification of police measures in favor of a more moderate political program. Underlying these points of dispute is the question of Mao's "leaning to one side" policy 25X1 [삭제: 두 줄가량 25X1로 지워졌다]

But despite these personal disagreements with party policy, a combination of factors -- the common interest that party and military leaders have in maintaining a united front, the strength of party organization, the highly centralized party control over the country's economic and military resources, and the narrowing of China's choice between alliance with the USSR and contacts with the West -- have all contributed to strengthening positive support for the party's present foreign policy by the higher political and military echelons of the Chinese Communist regime. Chang Kuo-t'ao, expelled

SECRET

Approved For Release 2005/04/26 : CIA-RDP79R01012A000800050020-5

from the Communist Party in 1938, has asserted recently that while differences may be assumed to exist over China's alliance with the USSR, individual leaders can still cooperate though holding different views on different problems. Not until the current course is discredited and domestic stability is seriously jeopardized can one expect the emergence of factors creating a possible cleavage between party leaders.

The prospects for the occurrence of basic disagreements and cleavages among the higher political and military echelons of the Chinese Communist regime arising out of developments in the Korean war are slight. The USSR has shown no signs of declining to place its military resources at the disposal of the Chinese Communist regime as a reserve of strength upon which the latter can ultimately draw if areas more intimately associated with its existence than Korea were attacked. As long as the Chinese Communist leaders have this assurance from Moscow they will probably accept, 25X1 with little significant dissension, whatever develops out of the Korean fighting.

B. Effect on Popular Support

It is difficult to isolate the Korean conflict from the complex of factors determining popular attitudes toward the Chinese Communist regime. The Korean conflict has been rarely, if ever, presented officially as a "foreign" issue, separate from the domestic scene, and the regime has sought to integrate the "aid-Korea" movement with its domestic political and economic program. Large segments of the population, principally in rural areas, probably have not yet consciously associated the war with the local problems with which they are most concerned; consequently, Korea probably remains to many an abstraction only vaguely comprehended.

Among the more politically aware groups, however, concentrated mainly in urban areas, the conflict has aroused a more definite, although mixed response. The available evidence indicates that, although some individuals privately have hoped that a Communist defeat would solve their difficulties, the most general and immediate reactions to the Chinese intervention and early victories were feelings of national pride evoked by impressions of a China restored to leadership rank in the Far East. The subsequent lack of military progress has quieted but not dispelled this exultation for even a successful holding action by Chinese troops against an array of strong Western armies has been viewed as a triumph compared to the long series of past Chinese humiliations. Communist propaganda concern about defense against the designs of Western powers bent on "invading" China has probably also gained some acceptance among these groups who have been most sensitive to foreign encroachments. The charge that the US is following in the footsteps of Japan and is resurrecting Japanese militarism

appears to

Approved For Release 2005/04/26 : CIA-RDP79R01012A000800050020-5
SECRET   I-5

appears to have achieved some effect even among those persons not inclined ordinarily to accept Communist propaganda. The student class as a whole seems to have exhibited the most enthusiasm regarding the Chinese role in the war.

On the other hand, doubts have arisen among the more educated and politically articulate groups, caused by feelings that the Korean adventure has jeopardized domestic reconstruction. There are also some reports that misgivings about the regime's pro-Soviet alignment and distrust of the USSR's intentions relative to the Korean situation have arisen among otherwise ardent supporters of the regime, including some party members.

The possibility that the Korean conflict may be merely a preliminary phase of a larger war is undoubtedly recognized by many in these groups, including some non-Communists who probably hope that, as a result, the regime will either be replaced or be forced to follow a more temperate course.

It is probable that in spite of Communist controls over the public information media, some knowledge of the Chinese losses in Korea has reached the general public (reports claim that some Chinese casualties of the Korean war have been transferred as far south as Canton). Presumably this knowledge has created either fearfulness or, in the case of anti-Communists, hopefulness, although firm evidence of specific effects is lacking.

Viewed in the larger sense, the domestic impositions and sacrifices which have coincided with the Korean war have made an adverse impression on the country even though these increasing hardships have not yet been correlated in the public's mind with the Korean war. In the rural areas,

conscription, production quotas, taxation, militia, and similar duties, and the greater reliance on force and suppression have all fostered dissatisfaction. In the urban areas, too, many of the same demands of the mobilization program have been felt heavily. In this indirect manner, therefore, the Korean war has contributed to a decrease in the degree of popular support for the regime, but this decrease does not yet constitute a serious threat to the regime's stability.

C. Effect on the Regime's Ability to Cope with Hostile Internal Forces

While intervention in Korea has required the regime to modify important phases of its planned political program, the regime has both the manpower and administrative machinery to continue and in fact step up the tempo of its efforts to consolidate control of the country. Its ability to cope with hostile forces has been demonstrated by the actual reduction, during the period of the Korean campaign, of active guerrilla-like elements.

Coincident with its aggression in Korea the regime also has broadened its suppression of alleged "internal enemies" who are regarded as seeking to dislocate China's domestic program and to undermine the People's Democratic Dictatorship in concert with American and Kuomintang agents. Ex-Kuomintang personnel and persons formerly associated with the Nationalist Government are a principal target of Communist repression. All available evidence indicates that Communist efforts to exterminate and paralyze potentially hostile elements have become increasingly pervasive and effective.

Repressive measures -- aimed at punishing espionage, sabotage,

conspiracy, subversion, collusion with "imperialists," instigating revolt and resistance, forgery and smuggling, harboring criminal elements, rumor-

mongering,

SECRET

Approved For Release 2005/04/26 : CIA-RDP79R01012A000800050020-5

Approved For Release 2005/04/26 : CIA-RDP79R01012A000800050020-5
SECRET   I-7

mongering, "and other crimes with counter-revolutionary purposes" -- have been reinforced by positive steps to strengthen the police and public security systems, to centralize and expand militia units, and to increase popular membership in the Communist-directed "people's organizations." These latter groups, an essential instrument of Communist control, not only function as surveillance and self-policing organs but they serve to fractionalize society and break up centers of potential opposition. Along with these measures the regime has steadily circumscribed the authority and power of non-party elite groups whose military and political services are no longer required. Moreover the recent declaration by a high party leader that the Chinese Communist Party "...is at present making preparations to carry out a systematic and all-out reorganization of the party organization" suggests that the regime's effort to weed out unreliables will extend with greater force than heretofore to the party itself.

As a result of these measures the regime has not only cut down active opposition but it has increased its ability to cope with potentially hostile forces.

D. Effect on Sino-Soviet Relations

Perhaps the most obvious effect of the Korean war on the foreign relations of the Chinese Communist regime has been the further estrangement 25X1

of the regime from the West and a concomitant increase [삭제: 25X1]

on the USSR, a dependence which Moscow has studiously en[couraged. 삭제: 25X1]

the outbreak of the Korean war a number of developments [삭제: 25X1]

which indicate that relations between Moscow and Pei-p'i[ng]

face at least, become increasingly amicable.

In the diplomatic sphere, there has been a close coordination of Chinese and Soviet positions and propaganda "lines" with respect to Taiwan, Korea, and Japan. Chinese Communist broadcasts continue closely to support Soviet views on such issues as the Japanese peace treaty. Stalin's self-interview of February 15, which was obviously intended to stiffen the Chinese Communist attitude on Korea, was promptly answered by a Chinese Communist editorial calling for an intensification of efforts in Korea. Meanwhile, the Chinese Communists continue to be shown a deference at formal diplomatic functions much greater than that accorded the diplomatic representatives of the Eastern European satellites.[1]

In the cultural and ideological sphere there have been similar signs of efforts to strengthen the ties between Soviet Russia and Communist China. Articles by Chinese Communist leaders have appeared with increasing frequency

in Soviet journals:

1. The Chinese Communist embassy reception at Moscow, celebrating the first anniversary of the Sino-Soviet Treaty, for example, was attended by a galaxy of high Soviet officials, including two members of the Politburo 25X1

[삭제: 25X1] and the full higher levels of the Soviet Foreign Ministry. [삭제: 25X1]

in Soviet journals;[1] the highest Soviet awards in the field of culture have been bestowed on Chinese citizens;[2] Soviet professors have been appointed to posts in Chinese Communist universities; and the membership and activities of the Sino-Soviet Friendship Association have been expanded.[3]

In the military and economic sphere there has been evidence of efforts to integrate Soviet and Chinese planning and operations. In December 1950, a top-level Sino-Soviet planning commission was reportedly established for the purpose of controlling and allocating strategic resources.[4] In March 1951, a further integration of economic and military operations was achieved by the signing of a Sino-Soviet railway agreement, hailed by the Pei-p'ing radio as a further step toward the full implementation of the Sino-Soviet Treaty of February 1950.[5]

Although the bulk of existing evidence would indicate that the course of Sino-Soviet relations has remained smooth, there are some indications that the economic and military cost of waging a protracted war in Korea may have generated certain strains in these relations, evidences of which are as follows:

(1) Information stemming from Anatoli Shabshin, former Soviet Vice-consul at Seoul, suggests that Mao was extremely reluctant to

While certain strains probably have developed out of the Korean war, there is no firm indication that they have yet become serious enough to threaten the solidarity of the Sino-Soviet alliance or to diminish Chinese Communist efforts in Korea. Both the Chinese and the Soviets have a common interest in driving US forces from Korea. Moreover, it is highly unlikely that the Chinese Communist intervention was prompted simply by Soviet promises and pressures. There exists an equally strong presumption that Chinese Communist action was prompted at least in part by motives of self-interest -- namely, a fear of US attacks on Manchuria, coupled with a chauvinistic and expansionist drive

toward territorial

toward territorial aggrandizement and in part by a genuine desire to further world Communist interests in the Far East, perhaps with a view toward increasing their own regional leadership role.

A clear indication of the present Chinese Communist attitude toward the Korean war was provided by the recent article of P'eng Chen, a member of the Chinese Politburo, published in the Cominform bulletin of April 27, and rebroadcast by the Chinese Communist radio on May 3. P'eng indicated clearly that the Chinese Communists regard the Korean conflict not merely as an isolated war of "self-defense," but also as an "integral" part of the global struggle between the forces of world Communism and the forces of imperialism, led by the "chief enemy," the US. As long as the Chinese Communists remain committed to this "subjective" view, and as long as they continue to subordinate considerations of economic reconstruction at home to the more general aims of world Communist expansion, there is little prospect of a serious weakening of their present allegiance to the Soviet camp.

I. 정치적 영향

가. 당 지도부 안의 이견

조선분쟁은 중국공산 측을 서방으로부터 고립시키고 소련에 더 밀접히 의존하도록 몰아감으로써, 중국공산당 안에 「민족주의」파와 「국제주의」파가 있다는 추측(어느 쪽으로도 확실한 증거가 없다)을 순전히 학술적인 물음으로 만들었다. 반면 조선 사태의 경과에 대한 불만이 중앙위원회 안에서 당의 재정·경제 정책, 재건 노력의 연기, 더 온건한 정치 강령을 위한 치안 조치의 강화를 둘러싼 다툼에서 비롯한 몇몇 이견점을 더 두드러지게 했을 가능성이 있다. 이 이견점들 밑바탕에는 마오의 「일변도」 정책 문제가 깔려 있다 25X1 [삭제: 두 줄가량 25X1로 지워졌다]

그러나 당 정책에 대한 이런 개인적 이견에도 불구하고, 몇 가지 요인이 겹쳐 중국공산정권의 상층 정치·군사 지도부 사이에서 현재의 대외정책에 대한 긍정적 지지를 오히려 강화해 왔다. 당·군 지도자들이 통일전선 유지에서 갖는 공동 이해관계, 당 조직의 힘, 국가의 경제·군사 자원에 대한 고도로 중앙집권화한 당의 통제, 그리고 소련과의 동맹과 서방과의 접촉 사이에서 중국의 선택지가 좁아진 사정이 그 요인들이다. 1938년 공산당에서 제명된

나. 대중 지지에 미치는 영향

조선분쟁을 중국공산정권에 대한 대중의 태도를 결정짓는 여러 요인의 복합체로부터 떼어 내기는 어렵다. 조선분쟁은 국내 사정과 분리된 「외국」 문제로 공식 제시된 적이 거의, 어쩌면 전혀 없으며, 정권은 「조선 원조」 운동을 국내 정치·경제 강령에 통합하려 애써 왔다. 주로 농촌지역에 있는 인구의 큰 부분은 이 전쟁을 자신들이 가장 관심을 두는 지역 문제와 아직 의식적으로 연관 짓지 못하는 것으로 보인다. 따라서 조선은 많은 이들에게 막연하게만 이해되는 추상적 관념으로 남아 있는 것으로 보인다.

그러나 주로 도시에 집중된, 정치적으로 더 깨어 있는 집단 사이에서는 이 분쟁이 더 뚜렷하나 엇갈린 반응을 불러일으켰다. 확보된 증거에 따르면, 일부는 사적으로는 공산 측의 패배가 자신들의 어려움을 풀어 주리라 바랐지만, 중국의 개입과 초기 승리에 대한 가장 일반적이고 즉각적인 반응은 중국이 극동에서 지도적 지위를 되찾았다는 인상에서 비롯한 민족적 자부심이었다. 이후 군사적 진전이 없었던 것이 이 고양감을 가라앉히기는 했어도 없애지는 못했다. 강력한 서방 군대들에 맞선 중국군의 성공적인 저지전조차 과거 중국이 겪은 오랜 굴욕의 연속에 견주면 하나의 승리로 여겨지고 있기 때문이다. 서방 열강이 중국을 「침략」하려 한다는 데 맞선 방어를 강조하는 공산주의 선전 역시, 외세의 잠식에 가장 민감한 이 집단들 사이에서 어느 정도 받아들여진 것으로 보인다. 미국이 일본의 전철을 밟아 일본 군국주의를 되살리고 있다는 주장은
